stepsRecall the energy stored in an inductor, U = 12 L I2, and rearrange it to L = 2U / I2 → Convert the given values to SI units: 25 mJ = 25 x 10-3 J and 60 mA = 60 x 10-3 A, so I2 = 3.6 x 10-3 A2 → Compute L = (50 x 10-3) / (3.6 x 10-3) and keep track of the power of ten to pick the option

Q2Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterRay Optics high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on applying the mirror equation for a concave mirror (image moves from 24 cm to 60 cm, i.e. 36 cm away from the mirror), which is ray optics.
subtopic 1Mirror Equation
why this subtopicThe answer comes from applying the mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f to a concave mirror (f = -15 cm) at u = -40 cm (v = -24 cm) and u = -20 cm (v = -60 cm), so the image moves 36 cm away from the mirror.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
An object is placed at a distance of 40 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm If the object is displaced through a distance of 20 cm towards the mirrors, the displacement of the image will be
  1. 36 cm towards the mirror
  2. 30 cm away from the mirror
  3. 30 cm towards the mirror
  4. 36 cm away from the mirror
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. 1f = 1v + 1q
  2. ⇒ -115 = 1v - 140
  3. ⇒ 1v = -115 + 140
  4. ⇒ v = -60025
  5. v = -24 cm
  6. Finally 115 = 1v1 - 120
  7. ⇒ -115 + 120 = 1v1
  8. ⇒ v1 = 3005
  9. So image is displaced by 36 cm away from mirror (d)

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Use the mirror formula 1v + 1u = 1f with f = -15 cm (concave).
  2. Initial position u1 = -40 cm: 1v1 = -115 + 140 = -8+3120 = -124, so v1 = -24 cm.
  3. Object moved 20 cm towards the mirror: u2 = -20 cm.
  4. 1v2 = -115 + 120 = -4+360 = -160, so v2 = -60 cm.
  5. The image shifts from 24 cm to 60 cm in front of the mirror: |Δ v| = 60 - 24 = 36 cm away from the mirror, which is option 4.

What catches a student
The trapoption 1Reversedreversedthe right thing stated backwards: direction, order or ratio

The two image distances come out right, 24 cm and 60 cm, and then the 36 cm is read as a movement towards the mirror because the object was moved towards the mirror

Who fallsa student who has solved both mirror equations correctly and takes the image to follow the object's direction of travel

Why it feels rightthe stem says the object is 'displaced through a distance of 20 cm towards the mirrors', so the only direction named anywhere in the question is towards the mirror, and the magnitude 36 cm is the right one

  1. okAt u=40 cm the image is at 24 cm; at u=20 cm it is at 60 cm.

No route to itoption 2

30 cm is not reachable from the printed numbers. The two image distances are fixed at 24 cm and 60 cm under either sign convention, so the answer is 36 cm; I then substituted the usual slips and none lands on 30 cm -- v=uf/(u+f) gives 10.9 cm and 8.6 cm, a difference of 2.3 cm; taking f as R/2=7.5 cm gives 9.2 cm and 12 cm, a difference of 2.8 cm; scaling the 20 cm by the magnification (v/u)2 gives 7.2 cm; and moving the object 20 cm the other way gives 4 cm. 30 cm is the second magnitude of a two-by-two grid of 30 and 36 crossed with towards and away.

No route to itoption 3

Same arithmetic as option 2: 30 cm is reached by no substitution into the mirror equation with f=15 cm, u=40 cm and u=20 cm, and this option carries the wrong direction as well, so it is the fourth cell of the 30/36 by towards/away grid.

  1. -x direction

Q4Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterRay Optics high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on refraction through a prism: the ray must hit the silvered face normally, so the refraction angle equals the prism angle (30 degrees) and Snell's law gives sin i = sqrt(2) sin 30 = 1/sqrt(2), i = 45 degrees, which is ray optics.
subtopic 1Prism
why this subtopicThe answer depends on prism geometry: to retrace its path the ray must strike the silvered face normally, so the refraction angle at the first face equals the prism angle (r = A = 30 degrees), giving sin i = sqrt(2) sin 30 degrees, so i = 45 degrees.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The refractive index of the material of a prism is 2 and the angle of the prism is 300. One of the two refracting surface of the prism is made a mirror inwards, by silver coating. A beam of monochromatic light entering the prism from the other face will retrace its path (after reflection from the silvered surface) if its angle of incidence on the prism is
  1. Zero
  2. 600
  3. 300
  4. 450
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. According to question
  2. Ray will retrace its path if r2 = 0
  3. Also,
  4. A = r1 + r2
  5. ⇒ 300 = r1
  6. By small law,
  7. u = sin isin 300
  8. ⇒ 2 = sin i12
  9. ⇒ i = 450

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. The ray retraces its path only if it strikes the silvered face along the normal, so the angle of incidence on that face is r2 = 0°.
  2. For a prism r1 + r2 = A, so r1 = A - 0° = 30°.
  3. Snell's law at the first face: sin i = μ sin r1 = 2 × sin 30° = 22 = 12.
  4. i = sin-1(12) = 45°, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict

stepsrecognise that retracing the path requires the ray to strike the silvered face along the normal, so the refraction angle at that face is r2 = 0 → use the prism relation r1 + r2 = A to get the refraction angle at the entry face, r1 = 30 degrees → apply Snell's law at the entry face, sin i = 2 x sin 30 degrees, to get the angle of incidence
why it is trickyThe work is turning 'retraces its path' into normal incidence on the mirrored face, then using r1 + r2 = A and one Snell's-law substitution with a standard surd value.
the catchTwo options are the results of wrong routes: 30 degrees is r1 reported as the incidence angle (skipping Snell's law), and zero comes from putting the normal-incidence condition on the entry face instead of the silvered face.

Q6Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterSemiconductor Electronics high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on how heating changes the V-I characteristics of a p-n junction diode, which is taught in Semiconductor Electronics.
subtopic 1VI Characteristics of PN Junction Diode
why this subtopicThe answer is that heating changes the overall V-I characteristics of the p-n junction (both forward and reverse behaviour), so it sits under V-I characteristics of the diode.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
In a p-n junction diode, change in temperature due to heating
  1. affects the overall V – I Characteristics of p-n junction
  2. affects only reverse resistance
  3. does not affect resistance of p-n junction
  4. affects only forward resistance
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. Due to heating, number of electron-hole pairs will increase, so overall resistance of diode will change.
  2. Due to which forward biasing and reversed biasing both are charged.

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. Heating increases thermal generation of electron-hole pairs, so the minority-carrier concentration ni2 ∝ T3 e-Eg/kT rises.
  2. In reverse bias, the reverse saturation current I0 rises with T, so the reverse resistance falls.
  3. In forward bias, the barrier potential V0 (knee voltage) falls with rising T, so the forward current at a given V rises and the forward resistance falls.
  4. Since both forward and reverse parts change, temperature affects the overall V-I characteristics, which is option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 highagree
difficultyeasy · 1 step
stepsRecall that heating increases thermally generated carriers in the semiconductor, which changes both the forward current (lower barrier/knee voltage) and the reverse saturation current, so the whole V-I characteristic shifts rather than only one branch
why it is trickyA single conceptual recall of how temperature changes carrier concentration in a p-n junction, applied to both bias regions at once.

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A then diamagnetic rod is placed vertically between the poles of an electromagnet when the current in the electromagnet is switched on, then the diamagnetic rod is pushed up, out of the horizontal magnetic field, Hence the rod gains gravitational potential energy. The work required to do this comes from.
  1. the induced electric field due to the changing magnectic field
  2. the current source
  3. the lattice structure of the material of the rod
  4. the magnetic field
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. Because when electromagnet is switched in the magnetic field associated with rod increases and leads to generation of induced electric field.

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · medium
  1. When the current is switched on, the electromagnet's field is set up by the external current source, which does work against the back-emf.
  2. The diamagnetic rod is repelled from the strong-field region and rises, gaining gravitational potential energy Δ U = mgh.
  3. As the rod moves, the flux linkage of the coil changes, inducing an emf that the current source must work against; the extra work it does supplies mgh.
  4. The magnetic field only stores and transfers energy, and the lattice and induced electric field are not energy sources, so the work comes from the current source, which is option 2.

difficultyhard · 3 steps
stepsRecall that a diamagnetic material is repelled from the strong-field region, which is why the rod is pushed up out of the field → Recognise that the magnetic field is only the agent that transmits the force and is not itself a reservoir of energy that can supply net work (a static magnetic field does no net work), and that the induced electric field and the rod's lattice are not energy sources here → Use energy conservation to trace the gain in gravitational potential energy back through the field to the external agent that sets up and maintains the field, and pick that option
why it is trickyThe work is a conceptual energy-accounting chain: recall diamagnetic repulsion, rule out the field and the rod's own material as energy sources, then follow energy conservation back to what powers the electromagnet.
the catchThe option 'the magnetic field' is exactly the result of the plausible wrong route of assuming that whatever exerts the force supplies the energy; seeing past it needs the non-obvious insight that the field only transfers energy from its source. The energy accounting (back-emf work done by the supply as the rod's magnetisation changes the flux) is not worked through in NCERT's Magnetism and Matter chapter.

solver reasoning: The energy to push the rod up is ultimately supplied by the current source that drives the electromagnet; the field only stores and transfers that energy.

Unpolarised light is incident from air on a plane surface of a material of refractive index ‘μ’ At a particular angle of incidence ‘I’, it is found that the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other, Which of the following options is correct for this situation?
  1. i = tan-1(1μ)
  2. Reflected light is polarized with its electric vector parallel to the plane of incidence
  3. i = sin-1(1μ)
  4. Reflected light is polarized with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. Since reflected & refracted rays are mutually perp
  2. So, μ = tan (i)
  3. So, Ans (4)

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Reflected and refracted rays perpendicular means i + r = 90°, so r = 90° - i.
  2. Snell's law: sin i = μ sin r = μ sin(90° - i) = μ cos i.
  3. Hence tan i = μ, i.e. i = tan-1μ (Brewster angle), so options 1 (tan-1(1/μ)) and 3 (sin-1(1/μ)) are wrong.
  4. At the Brewster angle the component with →E parallel to the plane of incidence is not reflected, so option 2 is wrong.
  5. The reflected light is plane polarized with →E perpendicular to the plane of incidence, which is option 4.

A body initially at rest and sliding along a frictionless track from a height h (As shown in the figure) just completes a vertical circle of diameter AB = D. The height h is equal to
  1. 54D

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. The circle has diameter AB = D, so its radius is R = D2.
  2. To just complete the vertical circle, the speed at the top B must satisfy vB2 = gR (normal force zero there).

  5. h = 52·D2 = 54D, which is option 1.

Which of the following carbocations is expected to be most stable?

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · medium
  1. Each structure is an arenium (σ-complex) ion formed when Y+ attacks nitrobenzene; label the carbon bearing -NO2 as C1.
  2. In a cyclohexadienyl cation the + charge is spread over the 1st, 3rd and 5th carbons of the pentadienyl chain, i.e. the carbons ortho and para to the sp3 carbon.
  3. Options 1 and 4 place + directly on C1, next to the strongly -I/-R NO2 group: highly destabilised.
  4. Option 2 has the sp3 carbon para to C1, so its resonance hybrid also has a contributor with + on C1: destabilised.
  5. Option 3 has the sp3 carbon meta to C1, so + is delocalised only over C2, C4, C6 and never sits on C1; the drawn + at C4 is also farthest from NO2 (weakest -I).
  6. Hence option 3 (the meta-attack σ-complex) is the most stable carbocation.

difficultyhard · 4 steps
stepsRecognise the four structures as arenium-ion (σ-complex) forms from attack of Y+ on nitrobenzene, and recall that -NO2 is strongly electron-withdrawing (-I, -M), so it destabilises a positive charge, most of all when the charge is on the carbon carrying NO2 → Read each ring to place the positive charge relative to the NO2-bearing carbon and the sp3 C(H)(Y) carbon → Eliminate options 1 and 4, where the positive charge sits directly on the carbon bearing NO2 → Choose between options 2 and 3, where the charge is off the NO2 carbon in both, by how far the charge is from NO2, using the fact that the inductive pull weakens with distance
why it is trickyThe work is reading four ring drawings to find where the positive charge sits relative to the NO2 group, using the electron-withdrawing effect of NO2 to rule out two options, then separating the last two by how far the charge is from NO2.
the catchTwo options (2 and 3) both keep the positive charge off the NO2-bearing carbon, so the usual rule that the charge must not sit next to an EWG leaves two candidates. The final choice depends on a finer argument about how the inductive effect falls off with distance and needs careful reading of the tilted ring drawings. The substituent Y is never specified, so the candidate must assume it is the same in every option.

solver reasoning: All four are sigma complexes of Y attacking nitrobenzene; only option 3 (meta attack) can never place the positive charge on the carbon bearing the strongly electron-withdrawing NO2 group, so it is the most stable.

The correct difference between first and second – order reactions is that
  1. the rate of a first order reaction does depend on reactant concentrations; the rate of a second order reaction does not depend on reactant concentrations.

  1. HBrO
  2. BrO3-

The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. +1HBrO ⟶ 0Br2, E°HBrO/Br2 = 1.595 V
  2. +1HBrO ⟶ +5BrO3-, E°BrO3-/HBrO = 1.5 V
  3. E0cell = E0HBrO/Br2 - E0BrO3-/HBrO

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. A species disproportionates spontaneously if E°cell = E°(its reduction) - E°(couple for its oxidation) > 0.
  2. For HBrO: reduction HBrO → Br2 has E° = 1.595 V; oxidation HBrO → BrO3- uses the couple E°BrO3-/HBrO = 1.5 V.
  3. E°cell = 1.595 - 1.5 = +0.095 V > 0, so HBrO disproportionates.
  4. For Br2: E°cell = 1.0652 - 1.595 = -0.5298 V < 0, not spontaneous.
  5. For BrO3-: E°cell = 1.5 - 1.82 = -0.32 V < 0, not spontaneous.
  6. BrO4- has Br in its highest state (+7) and cannot be oxidised, so it cannot disproportionate.
  7. Hence the species is HBrO, option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsRecall that disproportionation means one species is oxidised and reduced at once, so only an intermediate oxidation state can do it; this rules out BrO4- (+7, highest state) → For each remaining species (BrO3-, HBrO, Br2), set up the cell: reduction to the next lower species uses the potential to its right, oxidation to the next higher species uses the negative of the potential to its left → Compute E°cell = E(right) - E(left) for each species and pick the one where it is positive (spontaneous, ΔG° < 0)
why it is trickyThe work is reading a Latimer-type potential diagram: eliminate the highest oxidation state, then compare the right-hand and left-hand potentials of each intermediate species by one subtraction each to find a positive E°cell.
the catchThe diagram format and the 'right potential greater than left potential' rule are not taught as such in NCERT; the candidate must build it from the disproportionation definition (Class 11 redox) and E°cell = E(cathode) - E(anode) (Class 12 electrochemistry), and must remember to reverse the sign of the left-hand potential for the oxidation half.

  2. Low temperature and high pressure

  1. The reaction A2(g) + B2(g) ⇌ X2(g) has Δr H = -X kJ < 0, so the forward reaction is exothermic.

For the redox reaction
MnO4- + C2O42- + H+ → Mn2+ + CO2 + H2O
The correct coefficient of the reactants for the balanced equation are
MnO4-    C2O42-    H+
  1. 5    16    2
  2. 16    5    2
  3. 2    16    5
  4. 2    5    16
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)

  2. Oxalate ion n factor is 2.

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Oxidation states: Mn goes from +7 in MnO4- to +2 in Mn2+, a gain of 5e- per MnO4-.
  2. C goes from +3 in C2O42- to +4 in CO2, a loss of 2e- per C2O42-.
  3. Equalise electrons: 2 × 5 = 5 × 2 = 10 e-, so 2 MnO4- + 5 C2O42- → 2 Mn2+ + 10 CO2.
  4. Charge balance: 2(-1) + 5(-2) + x(+1) = 2(+2) ⇒ -12 + x = 4 ⇒ x = 16 H+.
  5. Hydrogen balance gives 8 H2O; oxygen check: 8 + 20 = 28 = 20 + 8.
  6. Reactant coefficients MnO4- : C2O42- : H+ = 2 : 5 : 16, which is option 4.

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Magnesium reacts with an element (X) to form an ionic compound. If the ground state electronic configuration of (X) is 1s2 2s2 2p3, the simplest formula for this compound is:
  1. Mg3X2
  2. Mg2X3
  3. Mg2X
  4. MgX2
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. X has 5 valence electrons hence it can form X3-
  2. The correct option is Mg3X2.
  3. Hence the correct option is 1

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. The configuration 1s2 2s2 2p3 has 5 valence electrons, so X gains 3 electrons to complete its octet, forming X3-.
  2. Magnesium loses its 2 valence electrons to form Mg2+.
  3. Charge balance: 3(+2) + 2(-3) = 0, so the formula is Mg3X2, which is option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsRead X's configuration 1s2 2s2 2p3 as a group-15 element (five valence electrons) and deduce the anion charge it takes on gaining electrons to complete its octet → Recall that magnesium (group 2) forms a dipositive cation → Combine the cation and anion charges into the lowest whole-number electrically neutral ratio and match it to the options
why it is trickyThe work is converting an electronic configuration into an ionic charge, recalling Mg's ion charge, and balancing the two charges into a formula: a recall plus a short charge-balancing application.
the catchOne distractor is the formula obtained by crossing the charges the wrong way round, which catches a candidate who balances carelessly; it does not change the band.

TypeMCQmcqa question and four answers, nothing lettered or listed
AsksRule appliedapply_rulea rule you already know, used on a case you have not seen
ConceptA 2p3 configuration means five valence electrons and an X3- ion, which balances against Mg2+ only in the ratio three magnesium to two X
Why this answerThis question requires a valency read off a configuration and turned into a formula, demonstrated by the stem's "ground state electronic configuration of (X) is 1s2 2s2 2p3" and "the simplest formula".
What catches a student
The trapoption 2Reversedreversedthe right thing stated backwards: direction, order or ratio

The two charges come out right, 2+ and 3-, and are then crossed the wrong way, so the 2 lands on magnesium and the 3 on X.

Who fallsa student who works out both charges correctly and then writes the subscripts without checking which charge goes to which symbol

Why it feels rightboth digits in the option are the right digits and they are the ones the charges supply, so the formula looks like the product of the right method

  1. okThe 2p3 configuration needs three more electrons, so X is X3-, and magnesium gives up two, so it is Mg2+.
  2. badCrossing them over gives Mg2X3.Each symbol takes the OTHER ion's charge as its subscript, so Mg takes the 3 and X takes the 2: Mg3X2, which also balances, three times 2+ against two times 3-.
Also pullsoption 4

Who fallsa student who writes the magnesium formula they write most often, MgX2, by analogy with MgCl2 and MgBr2, rather than working the charge out from the configuration

Why it feels rightMgX2 is the shape of nearly every magnesium formula met so far, so it looks like the simplest formula without any counting

  1. okMagnesium gives up two electrons, so it needs partners to take two in all.
  2. badSo two atoms of X take one each, giving MgX2.That assumes X takes one electron, like a halogen; this X has five valence electrons and takes three, which forces the three-to-two ratio.
No route to itoption 3

Mg2X needs X to carry a 4- charge against magnesium's 2+, and the printed configuration 1s2 2s2 2p3 has five valence electrons, so it completes its octet by taking three and cannot take four. The only two charges the stem makes available are 2+ and 3-, and those combine as three-to-two or, crossed the wrong way, as two-to-three; neither gives a two-to-one ratio, so no route reaches this option.

Q180Chemistry / physical
subjectChemistry
streamphysical
chapterThe Solid State high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the cubic unit-cell density relation (density = Z*M/(a^3*N_A)) with bcc edge a = 4r/sqrt(3) and fcc edge a = 2*sqrt(2)r, which is solid-state unit-cell calculation.
subtopic 1Density and Edge Length Calculations for Cubic Unit Cells
why this subtopicThe answer depends on the unit-cell density formula d = ZM/(a^3 N_A) with the edge length related to the atomic radius differently for bcc and fcc cells.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Iron exhibits bcc structure at room temperature Above 900°C, it transforms to fcc structure. The ratio of density of iron at room temperature to that at 900°C (assuming molar mass and atomic radii of iron remains constant with temperature) is
  1. 12
  2. 32
  3. 3342
  4. 4332
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. d1d2 = z1z2(a2a1)3
  2. The correct option is 3.

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. Density ρ = Z MNA a3; with M constant, ρ ∝ Za3.
  2. For bcc, atoms touch along the body diagonal: 3 a1 = 4r ⇒ a1 = 4r3, and Z1 = 2.
  3. For fcc, atoms touch along the face diagonal: 2 a2 = 4r ⇒ a2 = 22 r, and Z2 = 4.
  4. a13 = 64 r333 and a23 = 162 r3.
  5. ρbccρfcc = Z1Z2·a23a13 = 24·162 r3 · 3364 r3 = 3328.
  6. 368 = 3342 ≈ 0.92, which is option 3.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
33 highagree
difficultyhard · 4 steps
stepsRecall the number of atoms per unit cell for each lattice: Z = 2 for bcc and Z = 4 for fcc → Recall the edge-length to atomic-radius relation for each lattice: a = 4r/3 for bcc and a = 2*2*r for fcc → Write density = Z*M/(N_A*a3) for both phases and cancel M, N_A and r to get the ratio (Z_bcc/Z_fcc)*(a_fcc/a_bcc)3 → Substitute the edge lengths, cube the ratio of surds and simplify to match the radical form of the options
why it is trickyThe candidate has to recall two lattice parameters (Z and the a-r relation) for each of two cubic lattices, build the density ratio so that molar mass, Avogadro's number and radius cancel, then cube and simplify a ratio of surds.
the catchTwo distractors are the results of plausible wrong routes: option 4 is the inverted ratio (fcc to bcc instead of room temperature to 900 C), and option 2 is the plain edge-length ratio a_fcc/a_bcc, which is what a candidate gets by forgetting to cube it and to include the Z ratio.

AsksProportionalityrelationhow much one quantity changes when another does
ConceptDensity is ZM/(a3NA), so with the radius held fixed the bcc and fcc cells differ both in atoms per cell and in how the edge relates to the radius
Why this answerThis question requires the density expression applied to two cubic cells at constant radius, demonstrated by the stem's "assuming molar mass and atomic radii of iron remains constant with temperature" and four surd ratios as the options.
Noteasks is recorded as relation because the answer asked for is how many times the density changes between the two structures, and the options are that ratio rather than a value.
What catches a student
The trapoption 1Formula misusedformula_misusedthe right formula with a wrong power, a dropped term or the wrong quantity

Keeping only the atoms per cell, two against four, gives one half and drops the a3 term, where the two structures also differ.

Who fallsa student who remembers bcc as having two atoms per cell and fcc four, and treats density as proportional to that count alone

Why it feels rightthe atom counts are the one thing about these two cells that is remembered without working anything out, and their ratio is a printed option

  1. okA bcc cell holds 2 atoms and an fcc cell 4, and density goes up with the atoms in the cell.
  2. badSo the ratio of densities is 2/4 = 1/2.The cells are not the same size: with the radius fixed, a = 4r/3 for bcc and a = 4r/2 for fcc, and the cube of that difference has to go in too.
Also pullsoption 2

Who fallsa student who sets up the two edge-length relations correctly and then reads the density ratio straight off them

Why it feels rightthe surds 3 and 2 are exactly the two numbers the geometry supplies, so an option built from just those two looks like the geometric answer

  1. okWith r fixed, abcc = 4r/3 and afcc = 4r/2.
  2. badDensity goes inversely with a, so the ratio is 3/2.Density goes inversely with the VOLUME of the cell, so the surd ratio has to be cubed, and the atoms per cell still have to be put in: 12(3/2)3 = 33/(42).
No route to itoption 4

This is the keyed expression with the 3 and the 4 exchanged between numerator and denominator, and those two numbers enter the derivation from different places: the 3 from cubing 3, and the 4 from cubing 2 together with the two-against-four atom count. No single step moves one of them past the other. It is not the inverse of the key either, which would be 46/9, about 1.09, whereas this option is about 1.63. It completes the spread of surd expressions rather than ending a route.
